ANSWER: NOT TODAY, and not for the reason the question invites. The control relations all EXIST in the active chain -- artist_profiles.user_id (20240415000000:17), venue_profiles.user_id (:30), venues_v2.created_by (20250816133000:11), organizations.created_by (20250816132000:12) and org_members(org_id, user_id, role) (20250816132000:16-23) -- all asserted present by the harness. The obstacle is that NOTHING states what owner_id IS for a given owner_type, and the candidates are not one per owner_type.

WHAT THE FOUR POLICIES ACTUALLY CONSTRAIN, read from the chain and then EXECUTED. The four are exactly event_provider_connections_owner_read, _owner_insert, _owner_update and _service_role_all (20260927140000:211-260); a fifth, a DELETE policy, does not exist, and its ABSENCE is asserted as a positive claim by the contract rather than left as an observation. All three own-rows policies are `auth.uid() = created_by`; service_role_all is `USING (true) WITH CHECK (true)` scoped `to service_role`.

MEASURED, per policy, with the grant issued so the POLICY is the thing under test. READ: U1 (the creator) reads 1 row, unrelated U2 reads 0, and U1 reads the row even though its owner_id names an artist_profiles row owned by a third user U3 -- so owner_id is not part of the constraint. UPDATE: the chain grants authenticated SELECT only, so a first revision of this harness issued the UPDATE and read the resulting 42501 as 'the update policy constrains created_by'. It does not -- the GRANT refused before any policy ran. The harness now issues the UPDATE grant first, and then U1 matches 1 row while U2 matches 0 and the hijack does not land.

THE ABSENCE OF A DELETE POLICY, CONFIRMED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, and it is subtler than a refusal. With no DELETE grant the statement fails `42501 permission denied for table`. With the grant issued OUT OF BAND it does NOT fail at all: it is a SILENT ZERO-ROW NO-OP, because a DELETE whose USING filters every row away is not an error the way a failed WITH CHECK is. Fail-closed in both cases, which is why the migration's claim that disconnect preserves the row is sound, and asserted rather than believed.

THE THREE OWN-ROW WRITE POLICIES ARE NOT ON ANY LIVE PATH. All four writers resolve .from() through createServiceRoleClient() (bandsintown/connect:37, disconnect:22, events/[id]/claim:44, cron/events/sync). Measured: a service_role insert naming an owner_id the creator does not control SUCCEEDS and is readable; and with `grant insert, update ... to authenticated` issued out of band an authenticated insert naming a STRANGER's owner_id ALSO SUCCEEDS, because the WITH CHECK never mentions owner_id. The chain's grant is the only thing preventing the second case; the policy is not. That is the escalation primitive 20260927140000:285-289 already names in its own comment, and it is a boundary that is currently UNSTATED at the writer.

THE AMBIGUITY THAT BLOCKS THE DATA BOUNDARY, EXECUTED RATHER THAN ARGUED. 20260823010000_venue_identity_bridge.sql:36-44 declares a canonical identity TRIANGLE binding venue_profiles, venues_v2 and organizations as three DISTINCT mirrors of one account. Measured: the schema accepts a venue_profiles.id, a venues_v2.id AND an organizations.id under the same owner_type='venue' with zero refusals (5 rows stored, 3 distinct venue owner_ids), and an artist_profiles.id and a BARE auth.users.id under the same owner_type='artist'. Two defensible current-control resolvers, both implementable from the active chain, return DIFFERENT SETS for the same rows -- A `{V4, W4}` reading owner_id as the row's own relation, B `{O1, W4}` reading it as the venue mirror through the bridge. The organization arm disagrees the same way: organizations.created_by alone finds 1 controller, that plus org_members in ('owner','admin') finds 2. The chain has both conventions and picks neither for this table, so there is no single predicate to write.

WHY A RESOLVER CANNOT BE LIFTED FROM THE CHAIN'S ONE PRECEDENT. 20260825010000_ticketing_owner_account_resolution.sql had to build a 100-line resolver for a DIFFERENT column, and its own header records the defect it fixed: 'ownership only worked when the owner id happened to be a human auth user id'. Its venue arm is EVENT-SCOPED -- it reaches venue_profiles through events_v2.settings->>'venue_profile_id' or venue_identity_bridges -- and a provider connection has no event, so it cannot be reused even if the convention were settled. Writing a resolver here would be inventing the identity convention for a column whose convention the repository has never stated, which is exactly what 20260927140000:221-224 forbids: 'a schema-level owner check here would be invented authorization for a relation whose contract this file does not own'.

A FALSE ANSWER I ALMOST RECORDED, CORRECTED BEFORE IT REACHED THE RECORD. A first pass grepped the active chain for the control relations with a `public.`-qualified pattern, found none, and was about to conclude that the control relations do not exist. They do; the tables are declared unqualified in their own migrations. The near-miss is recorded because reporting a MISSING control relation where the real problem is an UNSTATED convention would have been the DB-017 error in a new place, and the harness now asserts the control relations' presence first so the tempting wrong answer cannot survive.

THE SINGLE CONSUMER RESPONSIBLE, NAMED: app/api/integrations/bandsintown/connect/route.ts. It is the only writer of owner_id (the table's three other consumers only read or update status) and the only point at which an unvalidated owner_id enters the table, which is why the ingress control and not the reader is the responsible consumer. Recorded in STATE.md, in proposed_decisions below, and in the handoff.

WHY THE ROW-LEVEL PREDICATE WAS STATED RATHER THAN WRITTEN, since the criterion also asks for it. The predicate that would make the existing policies sufficient is a conjunct of the form `auth.uid() = created_by AND <caller currently controls (owner_type, owner_id)>` on all three own-rows policies -- and the second conjunct is NOT WRITABLE today, for the three reasons AC-1 establishes: the id convention is unstated, two implementable resolvers disagree on the same rows, and the writer bypasses the policies entirely, so a new conjunct on them would change no reachable behaviour. It would add a per-row call to the one live caller-side reader (bandsintown/status, which has NO capability gate) and would be a fail-closed availability regression the moment the mapping is wrong. The predicate is therefore recorded as a requirement on the route and as the shape a follow-on migration must take, and NOT authored -- an invented conjunct is precisely what the read-only migration forbids.

THE DECISION IS AN ASSERTION, NOT PROSE, SO IT CANNOT BE INHERITED BY ACCIDENT. supabase/tests/db022_provider_ownership_contract.sql checks the three decision facts as POSITIVE claims: no foreign key on owner_id; no policy on the table references owner_id; no policy has command DELETE. An absent constraint and an absent conjunct are otherwise indistinguishable from a missing boundary, which is the exact failure DB-017 measured across the capability catalog (9 inert matrix grants believed to be enforced controls). Each violation message names the decision and says it must be re-derived.

THE THREE READERS ARE RECORDED AS MEASURED, NOT AS SECOND ORDERS. bandsintown/status:19 filters .eq('created_by', user.id) AND reads through the caller's own client, so the RLS read policy also applies; bandsintown/disconnect:32 answers 403 on created_by !== user.id; events/[id]/claim:73 added .eq('created_by', user.id) in EVENTS-004. Stated so that naming ONE responsible consumer is not read as exempting the readers: they carry the created_by bound, which is a DIFFERENT and weaker property than owning-account control, and the handoff says so.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: The created-time-versus-current-time property is addressed explicitly: created_by is a proxy for control of owner_id, and a connection created while a user legitimately held the account says nothing about who holds it now. Any predicate that relies on the proxy records that limit rather than implying current control.
evidence: EXECUTED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, because one direction alone is a claim the reader could dispute. Direction one, the security half: the seeded connection names an artist_profiles row owned by U3, U1 created it, and U1 can read AND UPDATE it although U1 has never controlled the account. Direction two, the availability half: transfer A1 to U1 and back to U3, and U1's access does not change in either direction -- the policy `auth.uid() = created_by` has no dependency on artist_profiles at all.

THE CONVERSE, WHICH IS THE HALF THAT IS EASY TO MISS: U3 DOES control A1 right now and is refused the connection for it, because U3 did not create it. So created_by is not a current-control test in EITHER direction, and a report that demonstrated only the first half would have understated the problem.

NOTHING EXPIRES THE PROXY. The table has no access-expiry, revocation or owner-verification column: asserted as a count of zero over those name patterns, so the claim is checked rather than asserted. created_at is the only recorded time for the ownership assertion, and it is CALLER-SETTABLE: U1 successfully re-pointed it ten years into the past with the UPDATE grant in place, so even the created-time is not an authority.

HOW THE LIMIT IS EXPRESSED SO IT CANNOT BE READ AS CURRENT CONTROL. Three places, all durable and none of them prose-only: (1) supabase/tests/db022_provider_ownership.harness.sh stage 5 is titled 'created_by IS A CREATED-TIME PROXY, NOT A CURRENT-TIME ONE' and executes the transfer in both directions; (2) the migration's own comment at :191 and the STATE.md entry both say created-time, not ownership; (3) the handoff's note_on_the_claim_route states it as the residual limit of EVENTS-004's fix, which is the exact place a future reader will look.

NO PREDICATE RESTING ON THE PROXY WAS AUTHORED, SO NO PREDICATE IMPLIES CURRENT CONTROL. The four existing policies do rest on the proxy and the contract asserts their exact rendered predicate, so the proxy is pinned rather than left to drift. The follow-on migration, if the convention is ever settled, must state the created-time limit in its own comment; the contract's column-set assertion (exactly 17 columns) is what forces that to be a deliberate edit, because adding an expiry column without recording the limit would be a contract violation.

### DB-022 — event provider connections: the owning-account check stays application-side (2026-09-28)

`public.event_provider_connections.owner_id` is a bare `uuid not null` with no foreign key and no owning-account column. Its four policies are own-rows predicates on `created_by` and on nothing else, and the deliberate ABSENCE of a DELETE policy is a decision, confirmed by execution rather than assumed. Measured on a throwaway instance against the chain's own bytes: a caller can read and update a connection naming an account they do not control, and a caller who DOES currently control that account is refused it, because `created_by` is a CREATED-TIME proxy and never decays.

**Decision.** The owning-account check remains purely application-side. The single consumer responsible for enforcing it is **`app/api/integrations/bandsintown/connect/route.ts`**, the only writer of `owner_id` and the only point at which an unvalidated one enters the table. Routed as `HF-DB-022-CONNECT-OWNER-VALIDATION` to integrations / INTG-008.

**Why not the data boundary.** Not because the control relations are missing -- `artist_profiles.user_id`, `venue_profiles.user_id`, `venues_v2.created_by`, `organizations.created_by` and `org_members` are all created by the active chain. Because **nothing states what `owner_id` IS**: `20260823010000` binds `venue_profiles`, `venues_v2` and `organizations` as three DISTINCT mirrors of one account, and the schema accepts all three under one `owner_type='venue'`, plus an `artist_profiles.id` and a bare `auth.users.id` under one `owner_type='artist'`. Two implementable current-control resolvers return DIFFERENT SETS for the same rows. Writing one would mean inventing the identity convention for a column whose convention the repository has never stated, which is what `20260927140000:221-224` forbids. And it would change no reachable behaviour anyway: every writer resolves `.from()` through the service role, so the three own-row write policies are not on any path today.

**Consequences to carry forward.** (1) The table's INSERT and UPDATE policies are decorative on current code; the GRANT is what denies, and a grant issued out of band immediately exposes a stranger-account insert. (2) A `DELETE` with no grant is `42501`; a `DELETE` WITH a grant is a silent zero-row no-op. Both fail closed, so `status='disconnected'` is the only retirement path. (3) `supabase/tests/db022_provider_ownership_contract.sql` asserts the three decision facts -- no `owner_id` foreign key, no policy referencing `owner_id`, no DELETE policy -- so a future migration that changes the premise turns the contract RED on purpose and must re-derive this decision rather than inherit it.

**Process finding, and it is the most reusable thing here.** The violation counter `grep -c 'as violation'` is VACUOUS: `as violation` is a column ALIAS, which tuples-only `psql` does not print, so the expression is always zero. It was reporting 'zero violations' while masking a real contract defect on a healthy target. The same idiom appears in at least one sibling contract harness in this repository; that lane's substantive `contains` negative controls did fire, so its conclusions stand, but the counter line is decorative there. Any contract harness that counts violations this way is measuring nothing, and a first clean run of one is the reason to distrust it rather than to believe it.

So AC-2 outcome B, exactly one of the two: the check stays application-side, and app/api/integrations/bandsintown/connect/route.ts is named as the single responsible consumer. AC-1's evidence is behavioural throughout: the four policies constrain created_by and nothing else, the absent DELETE policy is a silent zero-row no-op rather than a refusal, and the three own-row write policies are not on any live path because every writer uses the service role. AC-3's created-time limit is executed in both directions, including the half that is easy to miss -- a caller who NOW controls the account is refused the connection. checkpoints.summary: First full harness run: 340 checks, 13 failures, and four of them were defects in my own measurement rather than in the schema. (1) The UPDATE path was being measured through the GRANT: a caller-side UPDATE is refused 42501 because the chain grants authenticated SELECT only, so the first revision was about to conclude 'the update policy constrains created_by' from a refusal no policy had participated in. Fixed by issuing the UPDATE grant first, and the correction is recorded in the harness rather than quietly applied. (2) The absent DELETE policy was assumed to be a refusal; it is a SILENT ZERO-ROW NO-OP once the grant exists, because a filtered DELETE is not an error the way a failed WITH CHECK is. The harness now states the exact behaviour, which is more useful than the original claim. (3) The N1 control expected the chain's post-condition to raise UNEXPECTED; it raises the ABSENT list first, so the control was written against the wrong branch. (4) The N8 control expected a MISSING-contract-entries refusal and got the earlier RLS refusal instead, because the post-condition short-circuits. Split into two branches, which is the stronger control anyway.

checkpoints.summary: Instrument validation, and it found the most important defect in this task -- in my own work. With the chain's own post-condition validating the fixture, the first fully green run was 340/340. Because a first clean run is exactly the condition under which an instrument deserves suspicion, the same harness was run against two deliberately broken COPIES of the chain in a temp root. (a) Widening the read policy to USING (true) aborted the run at stage 1, as designed. (b) Adding an owner_id FOREIGN KEY in place, with no line shift, produced 19 failures: the chain's own post-condition stayed SILENT (it never enumerates foreign keys) while the db022 contract went red with the DECISION DB-022 message, so the decision is falsifiable and the instrument notices. Chasing a residual oddity in that mutated run then exposed TWO REAL DEFECTS IN MY OWN CONTRACT AND HARNESS: the violation counter `grep -c 'as violation'` matches nothing, because `as violation` is a column ALIAS that tuples-only psql does not print -- so it was always zero and had been reporting 'zero violations' the whole time; and it was masking a genuine contract defect, since the column comparison put information_schema's ARRAY against format_type's text[], so the `scopes` row could never match and the contract was reporting a violation on a HEALTHY target. Both fixed, plus a third gap the honest counter then exposed (a re-defaulted column still printed the summary row, so the summary now asserts the DEFAULT COUNT as well as the five defaults). The contract's 26 messages now carry a printed DB022-VIOLATION prefix, the type comparison is like-for-like, a dedicated pg_attribute text[] assertion covers what information_schema provably cannot see, and a POSITIONAL prefix-independent count is asserted beside the prefix count at every contract run. N11 is the control for the counter itself and is demonstrated moving to 1 and to 2. Final: 377/377, byte-identical across two runs.
